scenes.tts: Every pathway in this course has been running in your body the whole time you read it, but not all at once. Many of them are opposites that would cancel into a futile cycle. So the body switches them on and off in a timed sequence, as you move from fed to fasting to starving.
scenes.visual: Pathway chips; glycolysis and gluconeogenesis cancel in a futile cycle; chips resolve into a four-state timeline strip lit in order
scenes.narration: Every pathway in this course has been running in your body the whole time you read it, but not all at once. Many of them are opposites that would cancel into a futile cycle. So the body switches them on and off in a timed sequence, as you move from fed to fasting to starving.

scenes.tts: Watch the hours after a meal and you see a relay, each runner handing blood glucose to the next. Right after eating, glucose floods in from the gut and insulin rises. The message to every tissue is store. The liver lays down glycogen, and muscle takes up glucose. From four to sixteen hours, no more dietary glucose arrives, and glucagon rises. The liver now maintains blood sugar by breaking down its glycogen. That store is finite, and largely gone within about a day. By the end of an overnight fast, making new glucose already supplies roughly as much as glycogen breakdown does.

scenes.tts: Next comes fasting, at one to two days. With glycogen spent, the liver makes glucose from scratch by gluconeogenesis, drawing on lactate, the amino acid alanine, and glycerol. Meanwhile adipose tissue releases free fatty acids. These become the major fuel for muscle and liver.
scenes.visual: Liver, muscle, adipose chips; lactate, alanine, glycerol flow to liver which emits glucose; fatty acids flow to muscle and liver
scenes.narration: Next comes fasting, at one to two days. With glycogen spent, the liver makes glucose from scratch by gluconeogenesis, drawing on lactate, the amino acid alanine, and glycerol. Meanwhile adipose tissue releases free fatty acids. These become the major fuel for muscle and liver.

scenes.tts: In starvation, the brain is the problem child. It normally burns about 120 grams of glucose a day, and it cannot meaningfully oxidize long-chain fatty acids. They ride through the blood bound to albumin and are largely kept out of brain tissue. If glucose were the only option, the body would make all 120 grams by gluconeogenesis. The main raw material would be your own muscle protein. You would consume yourself within weeks.
scenes.visual: Brain with 120 g/day glucose need; fatty acids with albumin blocked at barrier; muscle protein pile drains through liver to supply glucose
scenes.narration: In starvation, the brain is the problem child. It normally burns about 120 grams of glucose a day, and it cannot meaningfully oxidize long-chain fatty acids. They ride through the blood bound to albumin and are largely kept out of brain tissue. If glucose were the only option, the body would make all 120 grams by gluconeogenesis. The main raw material would be your own muscle protein. You would consume yourself within weeks.

scenes.tts: Ketone bodies are the escape. They are small and water-soluble, and they cross into the brain. In starvation, the liver converts the flood of fatty-acid-derived acetyl-CoA into ketone bodies and exports them. Over several days the brain adapts to burn them, cutting its glucose requirement to roughly 40 grams a day. That protein-sparing effect decides whether you survive a long fast.
scenes.visual: Ketones pass the barrier; glucose need bar shrinks 120 to 40 g; muscle protein pile drains slowly
scenes.narration: Ketone bodies are the escape. They are small and water-soluble, and they cross into the brain. Over several days the brain adapts to burn them, cutting its glucose requirement to roughly 40 grams a day. That protein-sparing effect decides whether you survive a long fast.

scenes.tts: The liver makes ketone bodies but cannot use them. It lacks SCOT, the enzyme that reactivates acetoacetate so it can be burned. So everything it produces is shipped out to the brain, heart, and muscle. Ketogenesis is an export business.
scenes.visual: Liver with struck-out SCOT chip; ketone chips exported to brain, heart, muscle
